extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants (subject-matter-eligibility analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and tests for analyzing patent claim subject matter eligibility under the USPTO/ MPEP/Alice framework (Step 1, Step 2A prongs, Step 2B), with examples for claims involving neural networks, speech separation, and anomaly detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory Category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within at least one statutory category (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a series of steps it is a process (Example: 'The claim recites a series of steps and, therefore, is a process.'). Apply the plain meaning of claim language to decide category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recite an abstract idea and determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the two-part sub-test: (a) pick the specific limitations that may be abstract, (b) map them to MPEP groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes, certain methods of organizing human activity). Use claim language and plain meaning to identify the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Concepts (abstract-idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that recite mathematical formulas, transforms, or calculations (e.g., backpropagation, gradient descent, short time Fourier transform, explicit formula V = fθ(X)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recitations fall within the 'mathematical concepts' grouping of abstract ideas. Examples in the text: short time Fourier transform to form a spectrogram; using a formula to compute embedding vectors; backpropagation and gradient descent are mathematical calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes (abstract-idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that encompass mental observations, evaluations, or activities that can be practically performed in the human mind (e.g., 'detecting' anomalies, 'determining' association between anomaly and malicious packet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited activity can be practically performed by a human thinking/observing/evaluating data, it falls within the 'mental processes' grouping. Example: 'Detecting' encompasses mental identification; 'determining' may be performed mentally by evaluating packet data in light of detected anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity (abstract-idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract-idea grouping limited to specific sub-groupings such as fundamental economic principles, commercial/legal interactions, and managing personal behavior/interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expand this grouping beyond the enumerated sub-groupings in MPEP 2106.04(a)(3) except in rare circumstances. Evaluate whether the claimed activity fits one of the enumerated sub-groupings before categorizing it here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation; where claim language is silent, BRI may encompass any device or mechanism for performing the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under BRI, unspecified elements (e.g., 'receiving' audio, 'using' a DNN without details) are interpreted broadly to include any conventional mechanism; this can affect whether elements are considered conventional or merely generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that merely gather data or perform conventional, extra-solution tasks at a high level (e.g., 'receiving' input, 'transmitting' output) are insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label steps like 'receiving' or 'transmitting' as insignificant extra-solution activity per MPEP 2106.05(g) when recited at high generality; such elements do not integrate an abstract idea into a practical application by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions to Implement on a Generic Computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a computer or generic machine to perform an abstract idea without limiting how the computer/algorithm operates is mere instruction to apply the exception on a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that say simply 'using a DNN' or 'by a computer' without technical detail often amount to no more than instructing implementation on a generic computer (see MPEP 2106.05(f)). Such recitations fail to add significantly more than the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate those elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the additional elements apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception and results in a practical application (examples: real-time remediation steps that enhance security). If the claim as a whole reflects an improvement to a technical field, it may integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to Computer or Technological Field
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can be eligible if, as a whole, it provides an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technological field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show technical explanation in the specification and ensure the claim reflects the asserted improvement. Example: steps that act in real time to drop malicious packets and block future traffic can reflect an improvement to network security and thus integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Inventive Concept (Significantly More)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether additional elements are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity. If they are simply conventional use of generic components (e.g., generic microphones, generic DNN without details), they do not provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If background or common knowledge shows elements are routine (e.g., devices already equipped with microphones to receive audio), those elements cannot supply the inventive concept in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Claims Inherit Parent Limitations and Abstract Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim includes all limitations of its parent claim and thus inherits the abstract ideas recited in the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a dependent claim, consider the parent claim's abstract-idea findings; dependent limitations may add further elements but do not negate inherited abstract ideas unless they add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Reciting a Mathematical Concept vs. Being Based on One
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation that explicitly sets forth a mathematical concept (formula, transform) recites a mathematical abstract idea; a limitation that is merely based on such math but does not recite it may not be an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying binary masks or synthesizing waveforms may be based on mathematics but do not necessarily 'recite' a mathematical concept; likewise, limitations that cannot be practically performed in the human mind (e.g., synthesizing waveforms into time-domain audio) are not mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot Be Practically Performed in the Human Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation cannot be practically performed in the human mind (or via pen-and-paper), it is not a 'mental process' abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the limitation could be practically done mentally. Steps such as synthesizing audio waveforms or converting masked clusters into time-domain signals are technical operations that cannot be performed in the human mind and thus fall outside the mental-process grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Specification/Background to Support Claimed Improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the specification and background to determine if they describe a technical improvement and whether the claim reflects that improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the background explains an advantage (e.g., improved speech separation that does not require speaker-specific training and uses temporal/spatial features), that description can support finding the claim integrates an abstract idea into a practical application if the claim elements reflect those improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Drafting Guidance to Demonstrate Technical Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims to recite technical details showing how components (e.g., a DNN) achieve the asserted improvement, rather than merely stating 'using' generic components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include limitations that show how the algorithm/structure operates and how it modifies computer functionality (e.g., details of how the DNN aids cluster assignments, how masked clusters are synthesized into separate waveforms, real-time packet dropping/blocking), so the claim is more likely to be found to integrate the exception into a practical application or include an inventive concept.
